stem: A developer building with the Claude Agent SDK wonders if they still need to design their own guardrails (permission scoping, iteration limits, etc.) or if the SDK provides safe defaults requiring no further configuration. What is the accurate expectation?
explanation: While the SDK provides the building blocks (like a permission system) to implement guardrails, the developer is still responsible for actually configuring appropriate, task-specific guardrails (what permissions to grant, what limits to set) for their particular application, since the SDK provides the mechanism but can't know in advance what the right specific policy is for every possible use case.
reference: SDK provides mechanisms, developer configures policy

choices.text: The SDK provides the building blocks (like a permission system) to implement guardrails, but the developer is still responsible for actually configuring appropriate, task-specific policies for their application.
choices.reasoning: Correct: the SDK provides the mechanism for enforcing guardrails, but the actual, appropriate policy (what to permit, what limits to set) is inherently application-specific and remains the developer's responsibility to define thoughtfully.

choices.text: The SDK automatically provides fully safe, appropriate guardrails for any possible use case with zero configuration needed from the developer.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this overstates what any general-purpose SDK can provide out of the box; appropriate guardrail policy is inherently specific to each application's actual risk profile and requirements, which the developer must define.

choices.text: Guardrails are entirely unnecessary when using the Agent SDK, since the SDK itself eliminates all risk.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: using the SDK doesn't eliminate the underlying risks of autonomous agent behavior; thoughtful, application-specific guardrail configuration remains necessary.

choices.text: Guardrail configuration is only relevant if the agent uses extended thinking.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the need to configure appropriate guardrails is relevant to any autonomous agent's capabilities and actions, independent of whether extended thinking happens to be used.

stem: A developer wants to combine the sectioning and voting variants of parallelization in one system: split a document into independent sections (sectioning), and for each section, run its analysis multiple times and vote on the result (voting) before combining all sections' final answers. Is this combination valid?
explanation: Yes; the two variants address different aspects (dividing independent work vs. improving confidence on a single piece of work) and can be composed together, applying voting within each independently-sectioned piece to improve confidence on that specific section's result before the sectioned results are ultimately combined, which is a valid, more sophisticated composition of the underlying parallelization pattern.

choices.text: Yes; the two variants address different aspects (dividing independent work vs. improving confidence on one piece) and can be composed, applying voting within each sectioned piece before combining all results.
choices.reasoning: Correct: sectioning and voting solve different problems and are naturally composable, using voting to improve the reliability of each independently-sectioned sub-result before those results are ultimately combined.

choices.text: No; the two variants are mutually exclusive and can never be combined within the same system.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: there's no such mutual exclusivity; the two variants address different needs and can be layered together for a more sophisticated, combined benefit.

choices.text: This combination is only possible using the Batches API.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: combining these two variants works for real-time parallel calls just as well as batch requests; it isn't restricted to one specific processing mode.

choices.text: This combination always produces worse results than using either variant alone.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: there's no basis for this claim; combining the two variants for their respective, complementary benefits (independent decomposition plus per-section confidence) is a reasonable, often beneficial design.

stem: A developer has built a workflow and, separately, an agent for the same task, and wants a fair way to compare them before choosing one for production. Beyond just quality, what other dimensions should the comparison include, based on this domain's principles?
explanation: The comparison should also include cost (total tokens/dollars per task run), latency (time to complete), predictability/consistency across repeated runs, and debuggability/testability, since these are the dimensions repeatedly emphasized throughout this domain as relevant tradeoffs between workflows and agents, not just raw output quality in isolation.

choices.text: Cost, latency, predictability/consistency across runs, and debuggability/testability, since these are the tradeoff dimensions emphasized throughout this domain, not just raw output quality.
choices.reasoning: Correct: this reflects the domain's recurring emphasis that the workflow-vs-agent decision (and any comparison to inform it) should weigh multiple dimensions together, not evaluate quality in isolation from cost, latency, and predictability.

choices.text: Only output quality matters; no other dimension is relevant to this comparison.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this ignores the repeated emphasis throughout the domain that cost, latency, and predictability are all real, relevant dimensions alongside quality for this kind of comparison.

choices.text: Only which approach uses fewer lines of code in its implementation matters.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: implementation code length isn't among the substantive tradeoff dimensions (cost, latency, predictability, quality, debuggability) that matter for this comparison.

choices.text: This comparison should be based solely on which approach was built first, regardless of its actual measured characteristics.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: build order isn't a meaningful basis for choosing between two approaches; the comparison should be based on their actual measured performance across the relevant dimensions.
